masked entry point rather than to zero-size XPU tensors in general.

softmax (2, 0) is printed.

STEP 2 ok: F.softmax forward shape (2, 0)
STEP 2 ok: F.softmax backward grad shape (2, 0)
STEP 3 entering: torch._masked_softmax on shape (2, 0), dim=-1, mask_type=2
<no further output; process terminated by SIGFPE>

Environment
torch            2.16.0.dev20261006+xpu
python           3.13.13
device           Intel(R) Arc(TM) Pro B60 Graphics
xpu_available    True

(src/ATen/native/xpu/SoftMax.cpp:112 -> xpu::masked_softmax_kernel), so the
guard has to be added here; the upstream PR cannot reach it. The defect exists in
the current build independently of whether #199939 lands.

existing shape checks and before the dtype dispatch, so it matches
masked_softmax_backward_kernel and upstream masked_softmax_cuda:
  Tensor output = at::empty_like(input_, input_.options());
  ...
  if (input_.numel() == 0) {
    return output;

covered before #199939 brings test_masked_softmax_empty_dim into CI.

above.

issues.title: [xpu-alignment] [26-10-06] XPU kthvalue/median pick a tied index with a last-write-wins store, so kthvalue diverges from the first-occurrence index CUDA has returned since #165762
issues.body:
<!-- alignment-published-unit: pr-199947 -->
<!-- alignment-published-unit: pr-199947 -->
## Summary

XPU `kthvalue`, `median(dim)` and `nanmedian(dim)` pick the index of a tied value
with an unsynchronized last-write-wins store, so they do not return the first
occurrence of the selected value. For `kthvalue` this is a parity gap against
behavior CUDA has had since October 2025: upstream made CUDA `kthvalue`
deterministic and removed its non-determinism alert, while XPU still has the race
and still raises `kthvalue XPU does not have a deterministic implementation`
under `torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)`.

Observed on `Intel(R) Arc(TM) Pro B60 Graphics`, torch `2.16.0.dev20261006+xpu`,
python 3.13.13. On a 512x4097 float32 input whose median value repeats about 2049
times per row, all 512 rows returned a later duplicate:

| Reduction | Row 0 returned index | First occurrence | Rows wrong |
|---|---|---|---|
| `median(dim=1)` | 3647 | 4 | 512 / 512 |
| `nanmedian(dim=1)` | 1951 | 4 | 512 / 512 |
| `kthvalue(k=2049, dim=1)` | 1023 | 4 | 512 / 512 |

Every returned index did point at the correct value, so this is a tie-index
defect, not a wrong-value defect.

## Upstream source

- `pytorch/pytorch#165762` ("Fix race condition and make CUDA kthvalue
  deterministic") shows as CLOSED with no merge timestamp, but it **did land**:
  commit `79a4a9c02e73` (2025-10-25) is reachable from the default-branch head
  this scan froze (`512cddfdfe4504f5fcbf007141221a0ce20fc0b0`). At that head,
  `aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/Sorting.cu` `gatherKthValue` keeps a
  `__shared__ int32_t minIndexFound`, has matching threads take an `atomicMin`
  on it, and writes the result from thread 0 after `__syncthreads()`. The same
  commit deleted `alertNotDeterministic("kthvalue CUDA")` from
  `aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/Sorting.cpp` and removed `torch.kthvalue` from the
  CUDA list in the `use_deterministic_algorithms` docs.
- `pytorch/pytorch#199947` proposes the same `atomicMin` fix for `gatherMedian`.
  It is OPEN and UNMERGED, and `alertNotDeterministic("median CUDA with indices
  output")` is still present at the frozen head, so CUDA median is still
  documented non-deterministic.
- No `pytorch/pytorch` issue or PR owns the XPU half of either change, and no
  `intel/torch-xpu-ops` tracker covers it. `intel/torch-xpu-ops#5304` is about
  stale `alertNotDeterministic` calls in backward kernels and does not list
  `kthvalue`.
- Alignment scan window: `[2026-10-06T00:00:00Z, 2026-10-07T00:00:00Z)`.

## Root cause on XPU

`src/ATen/native/xpu/sycl/Sorting.cpp`, `gather_kth_value_kernel_func`
(lines 305-326): every work item scans its strided share of the slice, and each
one that finds a match writes the shared output itself, with no atomic, no
reduction and no barrier:

```cpp
  index_t kValueIndex = 0;
  bool foundKValue = false;

  for (index_t i = item.get_local_id(0); i < inputSliceSize;
       i += item.get_local_range(0)) {
    ...
    if (isKValue) {
      kValueIndex = i;
      foundKValue = true;
      break;
    }
  }

  if (foundKValue) {
    valuesSliceStart[0] = kValue;
    indicesSliceStart[0] = kValueIndex;   // line 325: concurrent store
  }
```

`gatherMedian` in the same file has the identical pattern at line 253
(`indicesSliceStart[0] = i;` inside the match loop). The stored index is
therefore whichever work item wins the race, which is why the returned index is
typically far from the first occurrence when the value repeats. The upstream
CUDA kernel fixed exactly this by reducing with `atomicMin` into shared memory
and having one thread store the result.

The dispatch layer reflects the current state:
`src/ATen/native/xpu/Sorting.cpp:197` still calls
`alertNotDeterministic("kthvalue XPU")`, and line 47 calls
`alertNotDeterministic("median XPU with indices output")`.

## Target-path evidence

- `torch.median(x, dim=1)` on the XPU input recorded
  `at::native::xpu::gather_median_kernel_func<float, unsigned int, 2>` under
  `torch.profiler` `ProfilerActivity.XPU`, and both values and indices came back
  on `xpu:0`, so the torch-xpu-ops sorting kernels serviced the reductions.
- Each returned index was gathered back out of the input and compared with the
  returned value before the index comparison, so a wrong-value failure would
  have been reported separately; all values matched.
- The expected first occurrence was computed as
  `(x == vals.unsqueeze(1)).float().argmax(dim=1)`, which is the documented
  first-maximal-index behavior, and it agreed on index 4 for row 0 across all
  three reductions independently.

## Reproducer

```python
import torch

ROWS, COLS = 512, 4097
g = torch.Generator(device="cpu").manual_seed(0)
base = torch.full((ROWS, COLS), 2.0)
n_side = (COLS - 1) // 4
for r in range(ROWS):
    perm = torch.randperm(COLS, generator=g)
    base[r, perm[:n_side]] = 1.0
    base[r, perm[n_side:2 * n_side]] = 3.0
x = base.to("xpu")

for name, fn in [
    ("median", lambda t: torch.median(t, dim=1)),
    ("nanmedian", lambda t: torch.nanmedian(t, dim=1)),
    ("kthvalue", lambda t: torch.kthvalue(t, (COLS + 1) // 2, dim=1)),
]:
    vals, idxs = fn(x)
    first = (x == vals.unsqueeze(1)).float().argmax(dim=1)
    print(name, "wrong rows", int((idxs != first).sum()), "of", ROWS,
          "| row 0 returned", int(idxs[0]), "first occurrence", int(first[0]))
```

Expected (the behavior CUDA gives `kthvalue`): `wrong rows 0 of 512`.

## Relevant output

```
MISMATCH median(dim=1) 512 of 512 rows returned a later duplicate; row 0 returned index 3647, first occurrence is 4
MISMATCH nanmedian(dim=1) 512 of 512 rows returned a later duplicate; row 0 returned index 1951, first occurrence is 4
MISMATCH kthvalue(k=2049, dim=1) 512 of 512 rows returned a later duplicate; row 0 returned index 1023, first occurrence is 4
```

## Environment

```
torch            2.16.0.dev20261006+xpu
python           3.13.13
device           Intel(R) Arc(TM) Pro B60 Graphics
xpu_available    True
```

## Scope and ownership

Both kernels live in this repository
(`src/ATen/native/xpu/sycl/Sorting.cpp`), so the work belongs here, but the two
halves are not equally urgent:

- **`kthvalue` is a current parity gap and the actionable part.** CUDA has
  returned the first occurrence and dropped its non-determinism alert since
  `79a4a9c02e73`; XPU returns a raced index and still raises under
  `use_deterministic_algorithms(True)` for an op the upstream docs no longer list
  as non-deterministic for any accelerator except MPS. This does not depend on
  #199947.
- **`median` / `nanmedian` should follow #199947 rather than lead it.** Upstream
  CUDA still alerts for median with indices output, so XPU currently matches
  CUDA; aligning median early would be fine but is not a divergence today.

Note on evidence limits: the reproducer stops at the first-occurrence
comparison, so run-to-run instability was not demonstrated at runtime. The
concurrent unguarded store at `Sorting.cpp:325` and the existing
`alertNotDeterministic("kthvalue XPU")` are the basis for calling it a race.

## Suggested direction

Port the landed CUDA reduction to `gather_kth_value_kernel_func`: keep a
work-group-local index initialized to `inputSliceSize`, have matching work items
`atomic_ref`/`atomicMin` into it, barrier, and store from local id 0; then drop
`alertNotDeterministic("kthvalue XPU")` from `kthvalue_out_xpu`
(`src/ATen/native/xpu/Sorting.cpp:197`) and add a first-occurrence test. Apply the
same shape to `gatherMedian` when #199947 lands, using a 64-bit shared index as
that PR does, since median allows slices longer than `INT32_MAX`.

_Filed with AI assistance (xpu-alignment automation); validated per the evidence
above._

issues.title: [distributed][launcher] torchrun --virtual-local-rank does not isolate devices on XPU (ZE_AFFINITY_MASK not set)
issues.body:
Found while porting `test/distributed/launcher/test_run.py` to XPU (pytorch/pytorch#182784): `--virtual-local-rank` doesn't isolate devices on XPU, so the test is skipped there for now. The details below were drafted with an AI assistant (Claude Code) and reproduced on our 4x Max 1100 machine.

> ### 🐛 Describe the bug
>
> `torchrun --virtual-local-rank` is meant to give every worker `LOCAL_RANK=0` and make its assigned GPU the only visible device. `LocalElasticAgent._set_local_rank_env` (`torch/distributed/elastic/agent/server/local_elastic_agent.py`) implements the isolation only through `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` / `HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES`. Intel GPUs ignore those variables and use `ZE_AFFINITY_MASK`, so on XPU every worker still sees all devices, gets `LOCAL_RANK=0`, and binds to physical device 0.
>
> Because of this, `test/distributed/launcher/test_run.py::ElasticLaunchVirtualRankTest::test_virtual_local_rank` passes on XPU without testing isolation: both workers really run on the same device. It is skipped on XPU in pytorch/pytorch#182784 until this is fixed. (#2717 was a different, already fixed failure of the same test.)
>
> Repro (`vlr_repro.py`):
>
> ```python
> import os
> import torch
>
> local_rank = int(os.environ["LOCAL_RANK"])
> torch.xpu.set_device(local_rank)
> props = torch.xpu.get_device_properties(local_rank)
> print(
>     f"RANK={os.environ['RANK']} LOCAL_RANK={local_rank} "
>     f"ZE_AFFINITY_MASK={os.environ.get('ZE_AFFINITY_MASK')} "
>     f"CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES={os.environ.get('CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES')} "
>     f"visible_xpus={torch.xpu.device_count()} uuid={props.uuid}"
> )
> ```
>
> ```
> $ torchrun --nproc-per-node=2 vlr_repro.py
> RANK=0 LOCAL_RANK=0 ZE_AFFINITY_MASK=0,1,2,3 CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=None visible_xpus=4 uuid=8680da0b-2f00-0000-2900-000000000000
> RANK=1 LOCAL_RANK=1 ZE_AFFINITY_MASK=0,1,2,3 CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=None visible_xpus=4 uuid=8680da0b-2f00-0000-3a00-000000000000
>
> $ torchrun --nproc-per-node=2 --virtual-local-rank vlr_repro.py
> RANK=0 LOCAL_RANK=0 ZE_AFFINITY_MASK=0,1,2,3 CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 visible_xpus=4 uuid=8680da0b-2f00-0000-2900-000000000000
> RANK=1 LOCAL_RANK=0 ZE_AFFINITY_MASK=0,1,2,3 CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1 visible_xpus=4 uuid=8680da0b-2f00-0000-2900-000000000000
> ```
>
> Expected: with `--virtual-local-rank`, rank 1 sees one XPU (`visible_xpus=1`) and it is physical device 1 (uuid `...3a00...`). Actual: both ranks see all 4 XPUs and run on physical device 0 (uuid `...2900...`).
>
> Suggested fix: in `_set_local_rank_env`'s virtual mode, also set `ZE_AFFINITY_MASK` to the worker's device, mapped through the parent's `ZE_AFFINITY_MASK` when set, the same way `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` is handled. Also update the `--virtual-local-rank` help text in `torch/distributed/run.py`.
>
> Closing criteria: this issue should only be closed once the `@skipIfXpu` on `test/distributed/launcher/test_run.py::ElasticLaunchVirtualRankTest::test_virtual_local_rank` has been removed and the test passes on XPU with real device isolation.
>
> ### Versions
>
> ```
> PyTorch version: 2.15.0a0+gite3fd018
> Is debug build: False
> OS: Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS (x86_64)
> Libc version: glibc-2.35
> Python version: 3.10.0 (64-bit runtime)
> Is XPU available: True
> XPU used to build PyTorch: 20260100
> Intel GPU driver version:
> * intel-opencl-icd: 26.27.39122.12-1290~22.04
> Intel GPU models detected:
> * [0]-[3] Intel(R) Data Center GPU Max 1100, driver_version='1.15.39122+12', total_memory=49136MB
> CPU: Intel(R) Xeon(R) Platinum 8480+
> [pip3] numpy==2.2.6
> [pip3] torch==2.15.0a0+gite3fd018
> [pip3] triton-xpu==3.9.0+gitb6f7ac74
> ```

issues.title: [XCCL] dist.isend blocks the host until the peer posts the matching receive; symmetric isend→irecv deadlocks
issues.body:
**Versions:** `torch==2.13.0+xpu` (torch-xpu-ops `bc294243`), `oneccl==2022.0.0`, 4× Intel Arc Pro B60, single node, Linux 7.0 / `xe`.
`CCL_ATL_TRANSPORT=ofi FI_PROVIDER=shm CCL_ATL_SHM=1 CCL_ZE_IPC_EXCHANGE=pidfd CCL_PROCESS_LAUNCHER=none`.

**What happens.** Two ranks, after a successful `all_reduce` on WORLD:

```python
peer = 1 - rank
w1 = dist.isend(send_t, peer)   # never returns on either rank
w2 = dist.irecv(recv_t, peer)
w1.wait(); w2.wait()
```

Both ranks block inside `dist.isend` (no error; our watchdog fires after 45 s with the last completed step being the WORLD `all_reduce`). With the order "lower rank: isend→irecv, higher rank: irecv→isend" the same exchange completes right away (the first exchange in ~35 ms, later ones in ~1 ms) and the data is correct.

**Why (from the code).** Since #3071 (`f09e211c`, "Add oneCCL groupStart/End for single P2P ops") every single P2P op in `ProcessGroupXCCL::pointToPoint` is wrapped in `OnecclGroupGuard`, and oneCCL's `group_end()` blocks the host until the operation has completed on both sides (event wait plus ack from the peer; see uxlfoundation/oneCCL#193). So `isend` is effectively a synchronous rendezvous, which breaks the non-blocking contract of `dist.isend` and turns the common symmetric pattern into a deadlock.

**Workaround that works for us:** `CCL_SEND=direct CCL_RECV=direct` — the symmetric isend→irecv pattern then passes (4 KiB and 16 MiB payloads, values verified), presumably because the SYCL pt2pt path is not used (as in pytorch/pytorch#156782).

**Ask:** either make single `isend`/`irecv` non-blocking again, or document that they block until the peer posts the matching op (and that `CCL_SEND/CCL_RECV=direct` avoids it).

nodes.body:
@AlexanderScha Having both ranks `isend` before either posts an `irecv` isn't guaranteed to work on either XCCL or NCCL. Point-to-point pairs that depend on each other need to go in one group, or they can deadlock. Instead of the direct workaround, use `batch_isend_irecv`, which is designed for exactly this case:
```python
peer = 1 - rank
ops = [dist.P2POp(dist.isend, send_t, peer), dist.P2POp(dist.irecv, recv_t, peer)]
for wk in dist.batch_isend_irecv(ops): 
    wk.wait()
```
For now it looks like there is a bug on our side if you put `irecv` before `isend`, so make sure you put `isend` first, and we'll track that issue separately.

Can you give that a try? Removing the group introduced in #3071 doesn't have any effect on this, in my tests.

ops = [dist.P2POp(dist.isend, send_t, peer), dist.P2POp(dist.irecv, recv_t, peer)]
for wk in dist.batch_isend_irecv(ops): 
    wk.wait()
For now it looks like there is a bug on our side if you put irecv before isend, so make sure you put isend first, and we'll track that issue separately.
Can you give that a try? Removing the group introduced in #3071 doesn't have any effect on this, in my tests.

nodes.body:
Thanks, that works. Same setup as above (`torch==2.13.0+xpu`, `oneccl==2022.0.0`, 2× Arc Pro B60, same environment, `all_reduce` on WORLD first), **without** `CCL_SEND/CCL_RECV=direct`. Each run does 3 exchanges and checks the received values with `torch.equal`; 3 runs per row:

| ops passed to `batch_isend_irecv` (both ranks) | 4 KiB | 16 MiB |
|---|---|---|
| `[isend, irecv]` | 3/3 pass | 3/3 pass |
| `[irecv, isend]` | 3/3 hang | 3/3 hang |

The `[irecv, isend]` hang is on both ranks inside `batch_isend_irecv` → `_coalescing_manager.__exit__` (`distributed_c10d.py:2928`), so it looks like the bug you mentioned. oneCCL logs `explicit dependencies are not supported for group calls: recv` there, but the passing order logs the same warning for `send`, so the warning is probably unrelated.

On #3071: fair point. We inferred that from reading the code and never tested a revert, so please disregard that part. Since `CCL_SEND/CCL_RECV=direct` also avoids the hang, the blocking is probably in oneCCL's default pt2pt path, not in the group guard.

A data point for the separate `irecv`-first issue: `omni/patches/sglang_diffusion_for_multi_arc.patch` in intel/llm-scaler replaces `batch_isend_irecv` in sglang's halo exchange with individual calls "for XPU/XCCL compatibility". The upstream op list there starts with an `irecv` from the previous rank, so that workaround may be for this same bug.

issues.title: Enable Windows XPU INT8/INT4 GEMM tests and extend INT4 group-size coverage
issues.body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

## The feature, motivation and pitch

The quantized GEMM tests in `test/xpu/test_linalg_xpu.py` have two coverage gaps:

- Four existing tests are skipped unconditionally on Windows, leaving the XPU INT8 and INT4 paths without numerical, compilation, and error-handling coverage from these tests on that platform.
- The eager INT4 test hardcodes `group_size=32`, so it does not exercise the supported group sizes 64 and 128. Group size affects weight quantization and the scales/zeros layout passed to the operator; testing only 32 leaves other weight-only quantization configurations uncovered. Group size 128 is particularly relevant to quantized LLM inference.

The proposal is to enable the existing XPU tests on Windows and extend eager INT4 coverage, without changing operator implementations or numerical tolerances. Windows execution results are required to establish that removing the platform skips is appropriate.

### Proposed changes

Remove `@unittest.skipIf(IS_WINDOWS, "Skipped on Windows!")` from:

| Test | Coverage | Existing parameterized cases |
| --- | --- | ---: |
| `test__int_mm` | INT8 x INT8 -> INT32, transpose and output variants | 16 |
| `test__int4_mm` | Eager INT4 packed-weight GEMM, BF16 and FP16 activations | 168 |
| `test_compile_int4_mm` | INT4 packed-weight GEMM with `torch.compile` | 8 |
| `test__int_mm_errors` | INT8 GEMM input validation | 1 |

Parametrize eager `test__int4_mm` over `group_size=[32, 64, 128]`, retaining the existing matrix dimensions and BF16/FP16 checks. Pass the selected group size to both weight quantization and GEMM. Explicitly skip cases where `K % group_size != 0`, since the quantization helper requires complete groups.

### Expected coverage

| Eager INT4 group size | Parameterized cases | Valid cases | Expected skips |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 32 | 168 | 168 | 0 |
| 64 | 168 | 140 | 28 |
| 128 | 168 | 112 | 56 |
| Total | 504 | 420 | 84 |

BF16 and FP16 are checked inside each valid eager INT4 case, not collected as separate test instances. The 336 added parameter combinations therefore provide 252 additional valid cases and 84 intentional skips. Skips correspond to `K=32` for group size 64, and `K=32,64` for group size 128.

Across the four tests, the expected total changes from 193 cases to 529 cases: 445 runnable and 84 intentionally skipped, before any environment-specific skips. The compiled INT4 test remains at group size 32; extending compiled coverage is outside this issue's scope.

### Validation and acceptance criteria

Run from the torch-xpu-ops repository root in a configured Windows XPU test environment, and repeat on Linux XPU:

```bash
pytest test/xpu/test_linalg_xpu.py -k "int_mm or int4_mm" -v -rs
```

For the INT4 subset:

```bash
pytest test/xpu/test_linalg_xpu.py -k "int4_mm" -v -rs
```

- All valid cases pass on Windows XPU, including eager INT4 with both BF16 and FP16 for group sizes 32, 64, and 128.
- Existing INT8 numerical/error checks and compiled INT4 checks pass on Windows XPU.
- No regressions on Linux XPU.
- Attach full logs or CI run links, exact commands, hardware/software versions, and explanations for any skips beyond the 84 invalid shape/group combinations. Explicitly confirm group-size-128 results.

These counts describe the parameterization, not a claim that hardware validation has passed.


### Alternatives

_No response_

### Additional context

_No response_

nodes.body:
Hello @guangyey, @CuiYifeng, @chuanqi129,

I wanted to ask you for advice - this issue wants to enable some tests on Windows that are passing on XPU hardware (details in description), but the upstream and local tests are gated with `@unittest.skipIf(IS_WINDOWS)`. So basically they are skipped on Windows in upstream, but it looks like Intel software allows to run them on Windows.

I was thinking about two solutions:
- Change `@unittest.skipIf(IS_WINDOWS)` -> `@unittest.skipIf(IS_WINDOWS and not TEST_XPU)`. This eventually require upstream changes in common test files and I haven't seen such solution yet anywhere.
- Create new test file in `torch-xpu-ops` `extended/` directory to cover those tests. This requires only local changes or upstream changes in the `xpu/` directory. This logically fits well, because it is extending the upstream default coverage to Windows for XPU hardware only.

What do you suggest? Maybe some other solution would be best? I wanted to ask you, because that is the first time I encountered case where we want to extend the Windows tests for XPU compared to PyTorch.

Came across this one when working on #4947. This isn't Windows- or LNL-specific: the file fails to collect on every OS since pytorch/pytorch#198121, and the fix is an 8-line deletion. Details below. @BartoszKokoszko, are you already on this? If not, I can open the PR.

### Analysis (AI-assisted)

**Root cause.** pytorch/pytorch#198121 (merged 2026-09-29, included in pytorch `release/2.15`) made `test/test_sparse.py` device-agnostic and renamed two tests that `test_sparse_xpu.py` retargets at import time: `test_cuda_empty` became `test_device_empty`, and `test_same_gpu` became `test_same_device`. `TestSparse.test_cuda_empty = retarget_outermost_onlycuda_to_onlyon(TestSparse.test_cuda_empty)` (line 133) now raises `AttributeError`, so the whole file fails to collect. The renamed upstream tests are `@onlyAccelerator`, so XPU runs them without a retarget.

**Impact.** The full sparse suite (about 6.1k tests) hasn't run in torch-xpu-ops CI since about 2026-09-30. The Linux BMG nightly 40343220345 (2026-10-26) shows the same collection error in both `op_ut` and `skipped_ut`. torch-xpu-ops `release/2.15` (pinned by pytorch `release/2.15` at `1dda266dd`) still has the stale lines, which matches the pt2.15rc3 report above. It also blocks re-verifying the sparse cases in #4947.

**Fix.** Delete the two retarget assignments (lines 133-135 and 143-145). Verified locally on Arc B580 against pytorch main (`a889cdc`): the file collects again (6170 tests), and `test_device_empty_xpu` / `test_new_device_single_device_xpu` pass. The multi-device variants are skipped on a single GPU. This needs a cherry-pick to `release/2.15` as well.

**Optional cleanup for the same PR.** The fork-local `test_Sparse_to_Sparse_copy_multi_gpu`, `test_new_device_single_gpu` and `test_new_device_multi_gpu` (lines 227, 252, 264) don't break collection, but they now duplicate upstream's `@onlyAccelerator` versions `test_sparse_to_sparse_copy_multi_device`, `test_new_device_single_device` and `test_new_device_multi_device`.

Automated fix session for intel/torch-xpu-ops#5620. Stages are appended below as they complete.
Issue Triage | Field | Value | |-------|-------| | Issue type | single-bug | | Reproduction missing | no | | Scope | torch-xpu-ops | | Dependencies | (none) | | Handling | agent-fixable | *Automated by issue-triage.*
Reproduce Reproduced on the latest XPU nightly wheel (`2.16.0.dev20261028+xpu`) with a `pytorch` `origin/main` source tree (`94fc3eeee66`) supplying `test/test_sparse.py`, on Arc Pro B60 (BMG). torch-xpu-ops at `73a6552c` (main). | Test case | Verdict | Observed | |---|---|---| | `test_sparse_xpu.py` (collection) | REPRODUCED | `AttributeError: type object 'TestSparse' has no attribute 'test_cuda_empty'` | The whole file fails at import time, so all ~6k sparse cases are lost, not just the two retargeted ones. This is not Windows/LNL-specific: the same error occurs on Linux/BMG here. *Automated by fix-reproduce.*
Root Cause Analyzed at `torch-xpu-ops@73a6552c`, pytorch `origin/main@94fc3eeee66`. `test/xpu/test_sparse_xpu.py` retargets a handful of upstream `@onlyCUDA` sparse tests at import time. Two of those lines read attributes that no longer exist on the imported class: `TestSparse.test_cuda_empty` (line 133-135) and `TestSparse.test_same_gpu` (line 143-145). Reading a missing attribute raises at module level, so the import fails and pytest loses the entire file (~6.1k cases), not just those two tests. Comparison of the Windows and Linux results; AI-assisted analysis is quoted below.

> | Measurement | Windows Eager | Windows Compiled | Linux Eager | Linux Compiled |
> |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
> | Memory (bytes) | 262,144 | 262,148 | 262,144 | 262,144 |
> | Memory (MiB, exact) | 0.25 | 0.2500038146972656 | 0.25 | 0.25 |
> | Memory (MiB, rounded to 1 decimal) | 0.2 | 0.3 | 0.2 | 0.2 |
> | FLOPs (normalized) | 0.3359375 | 0.3359375 | 0.3359375 | 0.3359375 |
>
> | Comparison | Exact Memory Difference | Rounded Memory Difference | FLOPs Difference |
> |---|---:|---:|---:|
> | Windows: compiled minus eager | +4 bytes | +0.1 MiB | 0 |
> | Linux: compiled minus eager | 0 bytes | 0 MiB | 0 |
> | Eager: Windows minus Linux | 0 bytes | 0 MiB | 0 |
> | Compiled: Windows minus Linux | +4 bytes | +0.1 MiB | 0 |
>
> The actual discrepancy is **4 bytes**. Python's ties-to-even rounding maps exactly `0.25` to `0.2`, while `0.2500038146972656` rounds to `0.3`, producing an apparent **0.1 MiB** difference. FLOPs are identical in all four cases.

***

### Analysis: `test_manual_ac` Eager vs. Compiled Memory Discrepancy (Windows vs. Linux)

#### 1. Should eager and compiled memory differ?
**No, they should not differ.**

`test_manual_ac` (`test/functorch/test_ac.py` / `test/xpu/functorch/test_ac_xpu.py`) tests that manual activation checkpoint boundaries (`checkpoint(f, x, use_reentrant=False)`) are preserved when auto-activation checkpointing (`activation_memory_budget=0.01`) is enabled:

```python
eager_mem, eager_flops = get_mem_and_flops(call)
mem, flops = get_mem_and_flops(call, memory_budget=0.01)
self.assertEqual(mem, eager_mem)
self.assertEqual(flops, eager_flops)
```

Both eager and compiled execution are intended to save the exact same activations across checkpoint boundaries (one tensor of shape `[64, 1024]` in `float32` = 64 * 1024 * 4 = 262,144 bytes = 0.25 MiB) and execute the exact same backward FLOP count (0.3359375).

The test rounds memory to 1 decimal place (`round(act_mem, 1)`):
- Eager (262,144 bytes = 0.25 MiB) rounds under Python's round-half-to-even rule to **`0.2`**.
- Windows compiled (262,148 bytes = 0.2500038... MiB) is strictly greater than 0.25 and rounds to **`0.3`**, triggering an `AssertionError: 0.3 != 0.2`.

---

#### 2. Root Cause of the 4-Byte Difference

##### A. Where do the 4 bytes come from?
In `test_manual_ac`:
```python
def call():
    return g(x).sum()
```
`g(x).sum()` returns a 0-dimensional scalar `float32` tensor. A scalar `float32` tensor on GPU/XPU occupies **exactly 4 bytes** of device memory.

##### B. How `get_act_mem` was intended to work:
```python
def get_act_mem(f):
    out = f()
    out.backward()
    start_mem = torch.get_device_module(GPU_TYPE).memory_stats()["requested_bytes.all.current"]
    out = f()
    cur_mem = torch.get_device_module(GPU_TYPE).memory_stats()["requested_bytes.all.current"]
    act_mem = (cur_mem - start_mem) / (1024 * 1024)
    out.backward()
    return act_mem
```
The helper assumes that because `out` is rebound (`out = f()`), the 4-byte scalar cancels out (+4 - 4 = 0 bytes):
1. In **Eager mode**, reassigning `out` in Python immediately drops the reference count of the old scalar tensor to 0. It is freed instantly by reference counting. Net scalar delta is 0 bytes, leaving only the 262,144-byte activation tensor alive at `cur_mem`.

##### C. Why Compiled mode holds the extra 4 bytes:
1. In **Compiled mode**, the first call to `f()` invokes TorchDynamo to trace and compile the frame.
2. Dynamo creates a **Python frame reference cycle**:
   `compile_wrapper` (`eval_frame.py`) <-> `CatchErrorsWrapper.__call__` / `_inner_convert` / `_compile` (`convert_frame.py`) <-> `frame`.
3. The local variable `result` inside the `compile_wrapper` frame holds a reference to the first call's 4-byte return tensor.
4. Because execution frames participate in a circular reference, standard CPython reference counting cannot free them—they can only be reclaimed when **cyclic garbage collection (`gc.collect()`)** runs.
5. In the second call `out = f()`, a second 4-byte scalar is created alongside the 262,144-byte activation tensor. Because cyclic GC has not run, the first scalar remains alive in the orphaned frame.
6. As a result, both scalar tensors are alive at `cur_mem`:
   `cur_mem - start_mem = 262,144 + 4 = 262,148 bytes`

---

#### 3. Why Linux and Windows Differ

- **CPython GC Generation 0 Threshold**:
  CPython runs generation 0 cyclic GC when object allocations minus deallocations reach `gc.get_threshold()[0]` (default 700).
- **Platform Heap Allocation Differences**:
  - On Windows, the number of Python heap allocations during Dynamo tracing for this small model leaves the generation 0 count at ~555 (under the 700 threshold). GC does not trigger between the first and second run, leaving the cyclic frame alive.
  - On Linux, platform-specific codepaths during compilation (POSIX path operations, dynamic linker resolution, subprocess handling, and compiler invocations) perform enough additional Python heap allocations to cross the 700 threshold. Cyclic GC triggers, reclaiming the orphaned frame before `cur_mem` is sampled.
- **Experimental Verification**:
  Invoking `gc.collect()` inside `get_act_mem` on Windows immediately drops the memory difference from 262,148 bytes to **exactly 262,144 bytes** (0.25 MiB -> `0.2`), matching Linux and Eager identically.

---

#### 4. Recommended Fix

In `get_act_mem` (`test/functorch/test_ac.py` and `test/xpu/functorch/test_ac_xpu.py`), explicit garbage collection should be invoked so uncollected cyclic compilation artifacts do not leak into device memory accounting:

```python
def get_act_mem(f):
    out = f()
    out.backward()
    del out
    gc.collect()
    start_mem = torch.get_device_module(GPU_TYPE).memory_stats()[
        "requested_bytes.all.current"
    ]
    out = f()
    gc.collect()
    cur_mem = torch.get_device_module(GPU_TYPE).memory_stats()[
        "requested_bytes.all.current"
    ]
    act_mem = (cur_mem - start_mem) / (1024 * 1024)
    out.backward()
    return act_mem
```

Because execution frames participate in a circular reference, standard CPython reference counting cannot free them—they can only be reclaimed when cyclic garbage collection (gc.collect()) runs.
In the second call out = f(), a second 4-byte scalar is created alongside the 262,144-byte activation tensor. Because cyclic GC has not run, the first scalar remains alive in the orphaned frame.
As a result, both scalar tensors are alive at cur_mem:
cur_mem - start_mem = 262,144 + 4 = 262,148 bytes


3. Why Linux and Windows Differ

CPython GC Generation 0 Threshold:
CPython runs generation 0 cyclic GC when object allocations minus deallocations reach gc.get_threshold()[0] (default 700).
Platform Heap Allocation Differences:

On Windows, the number of Python heap allocations during Dynamo tracing for this small model leaves the generation 0 count at ~555 (under the 700 threshold). GC does not trigger between the first and second run, leaving the cyclic frame alive.
On Linux, platform-specific codepaths during compilation (POSIX path operations, dynamic linker resolution, subprocess handling, and compiler invocations) perform enough additional Python heap allocations to cross the 700 threshold. Cyclic GC triggers, reclaiming the orphaned frame before cur_mem is sampled.


Experimental Verification:
Invoking gc.collect() inside get_act_mem on Windows immediately drops the memory difference from 262,148 bytes to exactly 262,144 bytes (0.25 MiB -> 0.2), matching Linux and Eager identically.


4. Recommended Fix
In get_act_mem (test/functorch/test_ac.py and test/xpu/functorch/test_ac_xpu.py), explicit garbage collection should be invoked so uncollected cyclic compilation artifacts do not leak into device memory accounting:
def get_act_mem(f):
    out = f()
    out.backward()
    del out
    gc.collect()
    start_mem = torch.get_device_module(GPU_TYPE).memory_stats()[
        "requested_bytes.all.current"
    ]
    out = f()
    gc.collect()
    cur_mem = torch.get_device_module(GPU_TYPE).memory_stats()[
        "requested_bytes.all.current"
    ]
    act_mem = (cur_mem - start_mem) / (1024 * 1024)
    out.backward()
    return act_mem

source.title: [XPU][Windows] Add explicit gc.collect() calls to obtain correct memory values

These tests are currently being refactored and ported upstream. test_linalg_batched_lu_stability_large_inputs is a CUDA-specific test (relying on cusolver) that gets erroneously instantiated on XPU via XPUPatchForImport.

In the upstream PR stack (culminating in pytorch/pytorch#197247), this test has been moved into TestLinalgCudaOnly (only_for=("cuda",)). Once PR #197247 merges, the test will no longer run on XPU and this issue will be resolved automatically.

We have infrastructure which supports local validation runs on the HW which is absent in the CI setup, such as ARC, MTL, see for example:
* [地址已移除]
* [地址已移除]

We've recently caught that some PRs modify CI setup without looking back at the above setups for non-CI hardware. This gives a high risks that the setup will get outdated and will require fixes before it could be used.

Proposal:

issues.title: [XPU] convolution_backward returns wrong gradients when grad_output is contiguous but has channels-last-looking strides
issues.body:
Found while enabling `test/functorch/test_ops.py` on XPU in [地址已移除：pytorch/pytorch#193412] `test_vmapvjp`, `test_vmapvjpvjp` and `test_vmapjvpvjp` for `nn.functional.conv3d` give wrong results on XPU and are xfailed there until this is fixed. I ran the repro below on an Arc B580 and confirmed the output.

The analysis, repro script and suggested fix below were produced with Claude Code (AI assistant).

> **Bug.** On XPU, `convolution_backward` returns wrong `grad_input` / `grad_weight` (errors of 10-40, in both float32 and float64) when `grad_output` passes `is_contiguous()` but `suggest_memory_format()` reports `ChannelsLast` / `ChannelsLast3d`. That combination is possible when a size-1 dimension has a non-canonical stride. functorch's conv batching rule produces such a `grad_output` under `vmap` with `in_dims=-1` on the cotangent (shape `(1, 2, 1, 1, 1)`, strides `(2, 1, 2, 2, 2)`), but functorch is not needed to hit it, and conv2d is affected the same way.
>
> **Root cause.** `convolution_backward_overrideable` picks the memory format from `use_channels_last_for_conv(input, weight)` and calls `make_contiguous_and_aligned(grad_output, mfmt)`, which is a no-op for an already-contiguous `grad_output`, so its strides survive ([Conv.cpp#L526-L534]([地址已移除])). The detail layer then recomputes the format from different tensors: `(src, diff_dst)` in `convolution_backward_weights` ([detail/Conv.cpp#L186]([地址已移除])) and `(diff_dst, weight)` in `convolution_backward_data` ([detail/Conv.cpp#L293]([地址已移除])). It picks channels-last and tags the oneDNN memory descriptors `ndhwc` on buffers laid out `ncdhw`. `.contiguous()` does not help because the tensor already counts as contiguous; `clone(memory_format=torch.contiguous_format)` does.
>
> **Possible fix.** Choose the memory format once in `convolution_backward_overrideable` and pass it down, or give `grad_output` canonical strides when its suggested memory format disagrees with `mfmt`.

Repro (no functorch needed):

```python
# XPU conv backward is wrong when grad_output is_contiguous() but its strides
# also look channels_last (only possible via size-1 dims). No functorch needed.
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def grads(x, w, g, dev):
    x, w = (t.to(dev).requires_grad_() for t in (x, w))
    return torch.autograd.grad(F.conv3d(x, w), (x, w), g.to(dev))

for dtype in (torch.float32, torch.float64):
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    x, w = torch.randn(2, 3, 6, 6, 6, dtype=dtype), torch.randn(1, 3, 3, 3, 3, dtype=dtype)
    g = torch.randn(2, 1, 4, 4, 4, dtype=dtype)
    g_odd = torch.empty_strided(g.shape, (64, 1, 16, 4, 1), dtype=dtype).copy_(g)
    assert g_odd.is_contiguous() and g_odd.contiguous().stride() == (64, 1, 16, 4, 1)
    ref = grads(x, w, g, "cpu")
    for tag, gg in (("canonical", g), ("odd", g_odd), ("odd.contiguous()", g_odd.contiguous()),
                    ("odd.clone(contiguous_format)", g_odd.clone(memory_format=torch.contiguous_format))):
        out = grads(x, w, gg, "xpu")
        print(dtype, f"{tag:30s}", [f"{(o.cpu() - r).abs().max().item():.3g}" for o, r in zip(out, ref)])
```

Output on Arc B580, torch 2.16.0a0+git5f3e475 (max abs diff vs CPU for grad_input, grad_weight). Both source files linked above are unchanged on main at 93dc3d4b5ff532bd84ee1b5839e6ed0f7019a61a.

```
torch.float32 canonical                      ['0', '5.72e-06']
torch.float32 odd                            ['17.8', '33.6']
torch.float32 odd.contiguous()               ['17.8', '33.6']
torch.float32 odd.clone(contiguous_format)   ['0', '3.81e-06']
torch.float64 canonical                      ['1.78e-15', '7.11e-15']
torch.float64 odd                            ['17.2', '39.8']
torch.float64 odd.contiguous()               ['17.2', '39.8']
torch.float64 odd.clone(contiguous_format)   ['1.78e-15', '7.11e-15']
```

issues.title: DLPack stream exchange is not implemented on XPU
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

=== 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch ===

`Tensor.__dlpack__` and `torch.from_dlpack` implement the DLPack stream handshake only for CUDA and ROCm. On XPU, `__dlpack__(stream=...)` checks that `stream` is an `int` or `None` and then ignores it: any integer is accepted, and no ordering is set up between the producer's current stream and the consumer's before the capsule is returned (the `self.device.type == "cuda"` branch in `torch/_tensor.py`). In the other direction, `torch.from_dlpack` passes `stream=` to the producer only when it reports `kDLCUDA` or `kDLROCM` (`torch/utils/dlpack.py`), so a `kDLOneAPI` producer is never asked to synchronize.

A DLPack exchange between XPU libraries that run on different queues therefore has no synchronization at the boundary, and callers have to synchronize by hand. The request is an XPU path equivalent to the CUDA one: when the consumer passes its queue, record an event on the current XPU stream and make the consumer's queue wait on it, and reject values that are not valid on XPU.

=== Alternatives ===

Keep XPU stream-unaware and document that consumers must synchronize (`torch.xpu.synchronize()` or an explicit event wait) before an exchange. In that case `__dlpack__` should reject any `stream` other than `None` or `-1` on XPU, as it already does on CPU, instead of silently accepting it.

=== Additional context ===

The array API standard leaves the stream type open for these devices: "For other device types which do have a stream, queue, or similar synchronization/ordering mechanism, the most appropriate type to use for stream is not yet determined. E.g., for SYCL one may want to use an object containing an in-order cl::sycl::queue." ([地址已移除]). The building blocks exist: a consumer can pass `torch.xpu.current_stream().sycl_queue`, and the producer can wrap it with `torch.xpu.get_stream_from_external`, the XPU counterpart of the `torch.cuda.ExternalStream` that the CUDA path uses. What is missing is the XPU branch in `__dlpack__` and `from_dlpack`, and an agreed convention for the stream value on SYCL.

pytorch/pytorch#195722 skips these tests in `test/test_dlpack.py` (`TestTorchDlPackDevice`) on XPU against this issue, as requested in [地址已移除：pytorch/pytorch#195722]

- `test_dlpack_conversion_with_diff_streams`
- `test_dlpack_conversion_with_diff_streams_narrow_precision`
- `test_dlpack_default_stream`
- `test_dlpack_convert_default_stream`
- `test_dlpack_cuda_per_thread_stream`
- `test_dlpack_invalid_rocm_streams`
- `test_dlpack_invalid_cuda_streams`

The first four call `torch.cuda.Stream`, `torch.cuda.stream` or `torch.cuda._sleep`, and the two default-stream tests also hard-code the default-stream values (1 on CUDA, 0 on ROCm), so enabling them on XPU means porting them to device-generic stream APIs, not only removing the skip. The last three check stream values that only mean something on CUDA or ROCm (2 is CUDA's per-thread default stream; 0 is invalid on CUDA, 1 and 2 on ROCm), so they need XPU counterparts rather than a port.

Issue Triage | Field | Value | |-------|-------| | Issue type | single-bug | | Reproduction missing | no | | Scope | unclear | | Dependencies | (none) | | Handling | agent-fixable | Two test cases (`test_memory_stats_xpu`, `test_memory_stats_multigpu_xpu`) fail from one cause: `torch.xpu.memory_stats()` does not report `num_sync_all_streams`, `num_device_alloc`, `num_device_free`. *Automated by issue-triage.*
Reproduce Nightly wheel `2.16.0.dev20261028+xpu` on PVC (Intel Data Center GPU Max 1550, 2 devices), test file from `pytorch/pytorch` `origin/main` @ `3afdbd3b95e`. Both cases carry `@skipXPUIf(True, ...)` pointing at this issue, so the markers were removed in-place for the run and the file reverted afterwards. | Test case | Verdict | Observed | |---|---|---| | `test_multigpu.py::TestMultiGPUDeviceXPU::test_memory_stats_xpu` | REPRODUCED | `AssertionError: -1 not greater than or equal to 0` | | `test_multigpu.py::TestMultiGPUDeviceXPU::test_memory_stats_multigpu_xpu` | NOT RUNNABLE HERE | skipped by the pre-existing `@unittest.skipIf(IS_LINUX, ...)` for `pytorch/pytorch#129860` | Direct confirmation of the gap: `torch.xpu.memory_stats()` returns no `num_sync_all_streams` / `num_device_alloc` / `num_device_free` key at all, so the test's `.get(key, -1)` yields `-1`. *Automated by fix-reproduce.*
Root Cause Analyzed at pytorch `origin/main@3afdbd3b95e`. `torch.xpu.memory_stats()` is built by `THXPModule_memoryStats` in `torch/csrc/xpu/Module.cpp:199`, which copies only the nine `StatArray` groups out of `DeviceStats` into the returned dict (`Module.cpp:231-241`). The scalar event counters that `c10::CachingDeviceAllocator::DeviceStats` declares -- `num_sync_all_streams`, `num_device_alloc`, `num_device_free` (`c10/core/CachingDeviceAllocator.h:55-63`) -- are never put in the dict, so the test's `memory_stats(device).get("num_sync_all_streams", -1)` returns its `-1` default and `assertGreaterEqual(num_sync_1, 0)` fails. The counters are missing at the source as well, not just at the Python boundary: `c10/xpu/XPUCachingAllocator.cpp` increments only `num_alloc_retries` (line 1025). The three sites that should bump them have no counter at all -- `alloc_block` (line 1055-1069, the `sycl::aligned_alloc_device` path), `map_block` (line 909-923, expandable segments), `release_block` (line 1132-1144), `unmap_block` (line 1206-1227) and `synchronize_and_free_events` (line 1075) -- and `resetAccumulatedStats` (line 1807) therefore resets only `num_alloc_retries`. CUDA keeps the same three counters next to exactly the corresponding trace records: `c10/cuda/CUDACachingAllocator.cpp:4450` (`alloc_block`, before `SEGMENT_ALLOC`), `:3880` (`map_block`, before `SEGMENT_MAP`), `:4593` (`release_block`, before `SEGMENT_FREE`), `:4713` (`unmap_block`, before `SEGMENT_UNMAP`), `:4759` (`synchronize_and_free_events`), reset at `:2832-2834`, and exposes them in `torch/csrc/cuda/Module.cpp:629-631`. The XPU allocator has a structurally identical set of functions, so the fix is to mirror those five increments, extend `resetAccumulatedStats`, add the three dict entries in the XPU `Module.cpp`, document them in `torch/xpu/memory.py`, and drop the two `@skipXPUIf(True, ...)` markers in `test/test_multigpu.py` that currently point at this issue. - **Verdict:** IMPLEMENTING -- a bounded CUDA-parity change entirely inside `pytorch` - **Target repo:** pytorch - **Domain:** upstream-pytorch *Automated by fix-root-cause.*
Implement Result - **Target repo:** pytorch - **Analyzed at:** pytorch@3afdbd3b95e - **What I changed:** `c10/xpu/XPUCachingAllocator.cpp` (+9) bumps the three counters at the five sites that already emit the matching trace record, and clears them in `resetAccumulatedStats`; `torch/csrc/xpu/Module.cpp` (+3) puts them in the `memory_stats` dict; `torch/xpu/memory.py` (+9) documents them; `test/test_multigpu.py` (-2) drops the two now-stale `@skipXPUIf` markers. - **Why:** the counters were absent both at the Python boundary (`torch/csrc/xpu/Module.cpp:233` copied only `StatArray` groups) and at the source (`c10/xpu/XPUCachingAllocator.cpp:1025` tracked only `num_alloc_retries`). Placement follows CUDA, which keeps each counter adjacent to the trace record for the same event: `c10/cuda/CUDACachingAllocator.cpp:4450` (`alloc_block`/`SEGMENT_ALLOC`), `:3880` (`map_block`/`SEGMENT_MAP`), `:4593` (`release_block`/`SEGMENT_FREE`), `:4713` (`unmap_block`/`SEGMENT_UNMAP`), `:4759` (`synchronize_and_free_events`), reset at `:2832-2834`, exposed at `torch/csrc/cuda/Module.cpp:629-631`. - **Scope note:** only the three counters this issue names. }); + stats.num_device_alloc++; record_trace( TraceEntry::SEGMENT_MAP, @@ -1059,6 +1060,7 @@ class DeviceCachingAllocator { TORCH_INTERNAL_ASSERT(p.block != nullptr && p.block->ptr != nullptr); + stats.num_device_alloc++; record_trace( TraceEntry::SEGMENT_ALLOC, @@ -1075,6 +1077,8 @@ class DeviceCachingAllocator { void synchronize_and_free_events( const std::shared_ptr& context, PrivatePool* pool = nullptr) { + stats.num_sync_all_streams++; + // This function syncs (event.wait()), so graph capture must not be @@ -1131,6 +1135,7 @@ class DeviceCachingAllocator { TORCH_INTERNAL_ASSERT(!block->expandable_segment); + stats.num_device_free++; record_trace( TraceEntry::SEGMENT_FREE, @@ -1217,6 +1222,7 @@ class DeviceCachingAllocator { } + stats.num_device_free++; record_trace( TraceEntry::SEGMENT_UNMAP, @@ -1820,6 +1826,9 @@ class DeviceCachingAllocator { stats.num_alloc_retries = 0; issues.title: Fused SDPA (OVERRIDEABLE / oneDNN) writes past its output buffer when q_len == 16 (head_dim 64, bf16, no mask)
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

On XPU, `scaled_dot_product_attention` with the default fused backend (`SDPBackend.OVERRIDEABLE`, oneDNN) returns NaN **and writes outside its output tensor** when the query length is exactly 16. The stray writes land in whatever the caching allocator placed next to the output, so other live tensors are silently corrupted.

Observed with bf16, 16 heads, head_dim 64, no mask, not causal. q_len 1, 4, 15, 17 and 32 are correct; only q_len == 16 fails, for every kv_len tried (128, 653, 773). `SDPBackend.MATH` and `SDPBackend.EFFICIENT_ATTENTION` are correct for all of these shapes. The result is deterministic.

```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
from torch.nn.attention import SDPBackend, sdpa_kernel

dev, dtype = "xpu", torch.bfloat16
H, D, KV_LEN = 16, 64, 653
torch.manual_seed(0)

for q_len in (15, 16, 17):
    q = torch.randn(1, H, q_len, D, device=dev, dtype=dtype)
    k = torch.randn(1, H, KV_LEN, D, device=dev, dtype=dtype)
    v = torch.randn(1, H, KV_LEN, D, device=dev, dtype=dtype)
    # Same-size blocks around the slot the output will reuse, so writes past its end land in a guard.
    guards = [torch.ones(H * q_len * D, device=dev, dtype=dtype) for _ in range(64)]
    guards[32] = None
    with sdpa_kernel([SDPBackend.OVERRIDEABLE]):
        out = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v)
    torch.xpu.synchronize()
    with sdpa_kernel([SDPBackend.MATH]):
        ref = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v)
    overwritten = sum(int((g != 1).sum()) for g in guards if g is not None)
    print(f"q_len={q_len}: output finite={torch.isfinite(out).all().item()}, "
          f"max err vs MATH={(out.float() - ref.float()).abs().max().item():.4f}, "
          f"guard elements overwritten={overwritten}")
```

Output:

```
q_len=15: output finite=True, max err vs MATH=0.0010, guard elements overwritten=0
q_len=16: output finite=False, max err vs MATH=nan, guard elements overwritten=1024
q_len=17: output finite=True, max err vs MATH=0.0010, guard elements overwritten=0
```

The overwritten values are bf16 NaN (`0xFFC0`).

**Impact.** This came up in a model whose scoring head cross-attends a few option queries over a ~700-token prompt (`nn.MultiheadAttention`, width 1024, 16 heads). Any input with exactly 16 options triggered it. The stray NaNs overwrote neighbouring small tensors (up to 16 KB in that setting), which caused NaN outputs on later, unrelated calls. In one long run they ended in a device assert that aborted the process. The same model is fine on NVIDIA GPUs. Restricting SDPA to `[SDPBackend.EFFICIENT_ATTENTION, SDPBackend.MATH]` avoids it with no measurable slowdown.

**Possibly related:** #5179 (fused SDPA leaves part of the output unwritten when kv_len is small) and pytorch/pytorch#195319 (oneDNN SDPA page fault with head_dim 64 and a rank-4 mask, reported safe for q_len ≤ 16). This case differs: q_len is exactly 16, there is no mask, and the kernel writes outside its output rather than leaving part of it unwritten.

### Versions

```
PyTorch version: 2.14.1+xpu (oneDNN v3.12.0)

issues.bodyText:
🐛 Describe the bug
On XPU, scaled_dot_product_attention with the default fused backend (SDPBackend.OVERRIDEABLE, oneDNN) returns NaN and writes outside its output tensor when the query length is exactly 16. The stray writes land in whatever the caching allocator placed next to the output, so other live tensors are silently corrupted.
Observed with bf16, 16 heads, head_dim 64, no mask, not causal. q_len 1, 4, 15, 17 and 32 are correct; only q_len == 16 fails, for every kv_len tried (128, 653, 773). SDPBackend.MATH and SDPBackend.EFFICIENT_ATTENTION are correct for all of these shapes. The result is deterministic.
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
from torch.nn.attention import SDPBackend, sdpa_kernel

dev, dtype = "xpu", torch.bfloat16
H, D, KV_LEN = 16, 64, 653
torch.manual_seed(0)

for q_len in (15, 16, 17):
    q = torch.randn(1, H, q_len, D, device=dev, dtype=dtype)
    k = torch.randn(1, H, KV_LEN, D, device=dev, dtype=dtype)
    v = torch.randn(1, H, KV_LEN, D, device=dev, dtype=dtype)
    # Same-size blocks around the slot the output will reuse, so writes past its end land in a guard.
    guards = [torch.ones(H * q_len * D, device=dev, dtype=dtype) for _ in range(64)]
    guards[32] = None
    with sdpa_kernel([SDPBackend.OVERRIDEABLE]):
        out = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v)
    torch.xpu.synchronize()
    with sdpa_kernel([SDPBackend.MATH]):
        ref = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v)
    overwritten = sum(int((g != 1).sum()) for g in guards if g is not None)
    print(f"q_len={q_len}: output finite={torch.isfinite(out).all().item()}, "
          f"max err vs MATH={(out.float() - ref.float()).abs().max().item():.4f}, "
          f"guard elements overwritten={overwritten}")
Output:
q_len=15: output finite=True, max err vs MATH=0.0010, guard elements overwritten=0
q_len=16: output finite=False, max err vs MATH=nan, guard elements overwritten=1024
q_len=17: output finite=True, max err vs MATH=0.0010, guard elements overwritten=0

The overwritten values are bf16 NaN (0xFFC0).
Impact. This came up in a model whose scoring head cross-attends a few option queries over a ~700-token prompt (nn.MultiheadAttention, width 1024, 16 heads). Any input with exactly 16 options triggered it. The stray NaNs overwrote neighbouring small tensors (up to 16 KB in that setting), which caused NaN outputs on later, unrelated calls. In one long run they ended in a device assert that aborted the process. The same model is fine on NVIDIA GPUs. Restricting SDPA to [SDPBackend.EFFICIENT_ATTENTION, SDPBackend.MATH] avoids it with no measurable slowdown.
Possibly related: #5179 (fused SDPA leaves part of the output unwritten when kv_len is small) and pytorch/pytorch#195319 (oneDNN SDPA page fault with head_dim 64 and a rank-4 mask, reported safe for q_len ≤ 16). This case differs: q_len is exactly 16, there is no mask, and the kernel writes outside its output rather than leaving part of it unwritten.
Versions
PyTorch version: 2.14.1+xpu (oneDNN v3.12.0)
OS: Microsoft Windows 11 Home (10.0.26200 64-bit)
Python version: 3.14.3 (64-bit runtime)

issues.title: Correct normalization of Dirichlet distribution
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

For multidimensional Dirichlet distribution it is expected that the output data sum up to 1. In floating point arithmetic some inaccuracies can be observed, however for XPU the difference is much bigger compared to CPU implementations. The noise propagates to backward computations and results in unacceptable noise level for gradient values

For cpu test does not exceed 1ulp with respect to unity. For xpu the maximum divergence is bigger
```python
import torch
a=torch.tensor([0.4,0.4,1]).expand(10000,3)
z=torch.distributions.Dirichlet(a.to('xpu')).rsample()
test = torch.max((torch.sum(z,1)-1)
```

### Versions

main

issues.title: [upstream_ut] test_cdist_backward_large_index GPU segfault: int32 overflow in XPU cdist backward buffer offset
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`test_cdist_backward_large_index` (test/test_torch.py, added upstream alongside the CUDA fix pytorch/pytorch#128791) causes a **GPU segfault that aborts the process** on XPU for both parametrizations:

- `test_cdist_backward_large_index_b_2_r_1024_m_2048_xpu`
- `test_cdist_backward_large_index_b_32_r_8192_m_1_xpu`

```python
import torch
b, r, m = 2, 1024, 2048  # also fails with 32, 8192, 1
dev = "xpu"
x1 = torch.randn(b, r, m, device=dev, requires_grad=True)
x2 = torch.randn(b, r, m, device=dev)
grad = torch.randint(-4, 5, (b, r, r), device=dev, dtype=torch.float)
(actual,) = torch.autograd.grad(torch.cdist(x1, x2, p=1), x1, grad)
```

```
Segmentation fault from GPU at 0xff0000020b800000, ctx_id: 1 (CCS) type: 0 (NotPresent), level: 2 (PDP), access: 1 (Write), banned: 1, aborting.
Abort was called at 288 line in file:
./shared/source/os_interface/linux/drm_neo.cpp
```

**Root cause:** in `src/ATen/native/xpu/sycl/DistanceKernels.cpp`, `cdist_backward_kernel_impl_func`:

```cpp
const int l_size = r_size * m;   // int32
...
scalar_t* buff_i = buff_data + l * l_size + (r1 * j + i) * m + init;
```

`l_size` and `l` are declared `int`. For `(b=2, r=1024, m=2048)`, `r_size = r1*r2 = 2^20`, so `l_size = r_size*m = 2^31` overflows int32, and `l * l_size` wraps, producing an out-of-bounds GPU write. The `(32, 8192, 1)` case overflows `dist.numel() == 2^31` similarly. This is the same int32 indexing bug fixed for CUDA in pytorch/pytorch#128791.

**Fix:** widen `l_size` (and `l`/`k`/`y`) to `int64_t`, mirroring the CUDA fix. `(r1 * j + i) * m` is already int64.

Because the failure is a process-aborting GPU segfault (not a catchable exception), the upstream test is skipped on XPU via `@skipIfXpu` referencing this issue.

### Versions

torch 2.15.0.dev20260923+xpu
GPU: Intel(R) Data Center GPU Max 1550

issues.title: test_split_with_sizes_copy_out_xpu crashes with Fatal Python error: Floating point exception (SIGFPE)
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`test/test_torch.py::TestTorchDeviceTypeXPU::test_split_with_sizes_copy_out_xpu` crashes the interpreter with a floating point exception (SIGFPE) on XPU.

Reproduce:
```sh
python test/test_torch.py TestTorchDeviceTypeXPU.test_split_with_sizes_copy_out_xpu
```

The test exercises `torch.split_with_sizes_copy` with out tensors, including cases with a zero-sized split (e.g. `(2, [3, 7, 10, 0, 30])`), which is a likely trigger for a divide-by-zero in the XPU kernel.

Output:

issues.title: [upstream_ut] test_bmm_matmul_mixed_dtype_error_xpu: mixed fp16/fp32 bmm/matmul does not raise
issues.body:
## Description
`test_bmm_matmul_mixed_dtype_error_xpu` expects `torch.bmm`/`torch.matmul` with
mixed input dtypes (fp16 @ fp32) to raise a RuntimeError, but on XPU the op
silently runs and returns a float32 result instead of raising. CPU/CUDA raise
`RuntimeError: expected scalar type ... but found ...`.

## Error log
```
test/test_torch.py:6868: in test_bmm_matmul_mixed_dtype_error
    with self.assertRaisesRegex(RuntimeError, "expected scalar type .* but found"):
AssertionError: RuntimeError not raised
```

## Reproduce
On a PVC machine:
```
python test/test_torch.py TestTorchDeviceTypeXPU.test_bmm_matmul_mixed_dtype_error_xpu
```
Minimal:
```python
import torch
a = torch.randn(2, 8, 8, device='xpu', dtype=torch.float16)
b = torch.randn(2, 8, 64, device='xpu', dtype=torch.float32)
torch.bmm(a, b)   # returns float32 on XPU, raises RuntimeError on CPU/CUDA
```

## Expected
XPU bmm/matmul should reject mismatched input scalar types with the same
RuntimeError as CPU/CUDA.

_Filed with AI assistance; reproduced per the details above._

issues.title: [upstream_ut] test_equal_xpu: torch.equal returns True for tensor containing NaN compared to itself
issues.body:
## Description
`test_equal_xpu` checks that a tensor containing NaN is not equal to itself
(`torch.equal(t, t)` must be False since NaN != NaN). On XPU the fast path
(same storage) short-circuits to True, ignoring NaN.

## Error log
```
test/test_torch.py:7048: in test_equal
    self.assertFalse(torch.equal(t, t))
AssertionError: True is not false
```

## Reproduce
On a PVC machine:
```
python test/test_torch.py TestTorchDeviceTypeXPU.test_equal_xpu
```
Minimal:
```python
import torch
t = torch.tensor([1., float('nan')], device='xpu')
torch.equal(t, t)   # True on XPU, False on CPU/CUDA
```

## Expected
`torch.equal` on XPU must return False when a tensor contains NaN, matching
CPU/CUDA (the same-storage fast path must not skip the NaN check).

_Filed with AI assistance; reproduced per the details above._

> `arange` support for XPU, then remove the corresponding test skips.

issues.title: sdpa in QwenImage VAE need 16G memory in xpu, while cuda only need 0.09G memory in A100
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

```
import argparse

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F


parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Measure QwenImage VAE SDPA memory use")
parser.add_argument("--device", choices=("cuda", "xpu"), required=True)
args = parser.parse_args()

device = args.device
accelerator = getattr(torch, device, None)
if accelerator is None or not accelerator.is_available():
    parser.error(f"{device} is not available")

accelerator.empty_cache()
accelerator.reset_peak_memory_stats()
qkv = torch.randn(1, 1, 65536, 288, device=device, dtype=torch.float32)
query, key, value = qkv.chunk(3, dim=-1)

print(f"torch={torch.__version__} device={accelerator.get_device_name(0)} backend=default", flush=True)
print(f"q/k/v shape={tuple(query.shape)} stride={query.stride()} dtype={query.dtype}", flush=True)

try:
    output = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(query, key, value)
    accelerator.synchronize()
    print(f"output shape={tuple(output.shape)}", flush=True)
finally:
    print(
        f"peak allocated={accelerator.max_memory_allocated() / 1024**3:.2f} GiB "
        f"peak reserved={accelerator.max_memory_reserved() / 1024**3:.2f} GiB",
        flush=True,
    )
```

issues.title: `torch.xpu.Event.elapsed_time` silently succeeds for events recorded on different devices (CUDA raises)
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`torch.cuda.Event.elapsed_time` rejects a pair of events that were recorded on different devices:  cudaEventElapsedTime` returns `cudaErrorInvalidResourceHandle`, which surfaces as a `RuntimeError`. `torch.xpu.Event.elapsed_time` has no equivalent check and returns a number instead.

The XPU implementation subtracts the two events' `command_end` profiling values directly, without consulting either event's device (`c10/xpu/XPUEvent.h`, `elapsed_time`):

```cpp
using namespace sycl::info::event_profiling;
uint64_t end_time_ns = other.event().get_profiling_info<command_end>();
uint64_t start_time_ns = event().get_profiling_info<command_end>();
return 1e-6 * (static_cast<double>(end_time_ns) - static_cast<double>(start_time_ns));
```

The generic accelerator path does the same: `XPUGuardImpl::elapsedTime` (`c10/xpu/impl/XPUGuardImpl.h`) accepts a `device_index` argument but never uses it, so `torch.Event.elapsed_time` behaves identically.

SYCL defines `command_end` as a timestamp in nanoseconds since an implementation-defined epoch, and we could not find anything in PyTorch that normalizes per-device timestamps onto a shared timebase (no use of
`zeDeviceGetGlobalTimestamps` or equivalent in `c10/xpu`, `aten/src/ATen/xpu`, or `torch/csrc/xpu`). If the two devices do not share a time domain, the subtraction crosses epochs and the returned value is not a meaningful duration -- but silently looks like one.

We are not asserting that the number is wrong, only that its semantics are currently unspecified. Either outcome would be fine, we just need it defined:

- **Raise**, matching CUDA, so cross-device misuse is reported rather than silently producing a plausible-looking float; or
- **Document that it is supported**, and state the timebase guarantee that makes the result meaningful across devices.

### Reproducer

Requires two XPU devices.

```python
import torch

d0, d1 = "xpu:0", "xpu:1"

with torch.xpu.device(d0):
    s0 = torch.xpu.current_stream()
    e0 = torch.xpu.Event(enable_timing=True)
    torch.randn(4096, 4096, device=d0).sum()
    s0.record_event(e0)

with torch.xpu.device(d1):
    s1 = torch.xpu.current_stream()
    e1 = torch.xpu.Event(enable_timing=True)
    torch.randn(4096, 4096, device=d1).sum()
    s1.record_event(e1)

e0.synchronize()
e1.synchronize()

# CUDA raises RuntimeError here. XPU returns a float.
print("cross-device elapsed_time:", e0.elapsed_time(e1))
```

Observed on XPU: a float is printed.

Expected (CUDA behaviour for comparison, substituting `cuda` for `xpu`):

```
RuntimeError: CUDA error: invalid resource handle
```

### Why this matters now

`test/test_cuda_multigpu.py::TestCudaMultiGPU::test_events_multi_gpu_elapsed_time`
asserts the CUDA behaviour:

```python
with self.assertRaises(RuntimeError):
    self.assertGreater(e0.elapsed_time(e1), 0)
```

That test is being made device-generic in [地址已移除：pytorch/pytorch#197241] (the file is renamed to
`test/test_multigpu.py`). The cross-device half cannot be enabled for XPU while the behaviours differ, so it is skipped on XPU pending the outcome of this issue.

Note that the rest of the test is device-agnostic and does pass on XPU: two events recorded on the *same* device, with `elapsed_time` queried while a *different* device is current. Only the cross-device-events case diverges.

issues.title: [TorchAO][BMG] WW41 WOQ INT4 total latency regressions (>5%) across 10 cases
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

On Intel Arc B580 (BMG), 10 TorchAO WOQ INT4 inference configurations have **more than 5% higher total latency in WW41 than WW38**. All measurements below use 1024 input / 1024 output tokens, SDPA, FP16 activations, and batch size (bs) 1 or 8. The comparison is from the WW41 weekly performance workbook (`torchao_ww41.xlsx`, `summary` sheet, WW38 vs WW41 columns); increase = `(WW41 / WW38 - 1) × 100%`. This is an end-to-end total-latency regression, not a first-token-latency regression.

| WOQ INT4 | Model | bs | WW38 total latency (s) | WW41 total latency (s) | Increase |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |

Our investigation shows that part of the XPU decoding performance regression is related to PyTorch pytorch/pytorch#190986, and is consistent with the same issue in intel/torch-xpu-ops#5543.

The corresponding issue has been fixed in the latest XPU nightly. Our validation shows that the performance has partially recovered:

| Regression build (WW41) | 7,398,168 ns |
| Latest XPU nightly | 7,114,505 ns |

The latest nightly improves the regression relative to WW41, but it has not yet returned to the baseline level. A measurable performance gap remains, and we are continuing to investigate the remaining difference.

We will provide another update once the remaining performance gap is understood and validated.

issues.title: [xpu-alignment] [26-10-12] XPU copy_ double-applies conj/neg view bits when a broadcasting CPU<->XPU copy requires temporary staging
issues.body:
<!-- alignment-published-unit: issue-200613 -->
## Summary

A blocking `Tensor.copy_` of a conjugate (or negative) view across the CPU/XPU
boundary writes the view's *physical* values instead of its logical values
whenever broadcasting forces temporary staging. The copy completes without
raising; only the sign is wrong, so this is a silent-correctness bug.

Found by an upstream-alignment scan of `pytorch/pytorch` over the UTC window
`[2026-10-12T00:00:00Z, 2026-10-13T00:00:00Z)`.

**Upstream source:** [地址已移除：pytorch/pytorch#200613] - reported
against ROCm and blaming `aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/Copy.cu`. The issue is open,
has no linked fix PR, and never mentions XPU. `src/ATen/native/xpu/Copy.cpp`
carries an independent copy of the same staging branch, so an upstream fix to
`Copy.cu` would not fix XPU.

## Observed XPU behavior

| Direction | Source view | Actual | Expected |
|---|---|---|---|
| cpu -> xpu | `z.conj()` | `[(1+2j), (1+2j)]` | `[(1-2j), (1-2j)]` |
| cpu -> xpu | `z.conj().imag` | `[2.0, 2.0]` | `[-2.0, -2.0]` |
| xpu -> cpu | `z.conj()` | `[(1+2j), (1+2j)]` | `[(1-2j), (1-2j)]` |
| xpu -> cpu | `z.conj().imag` | `[2.0, 2.0]` | `[-2.0, -2.0]` |
| xpu -> xpu | both | correct | correct |

In every failing case the value written is exactly the source's physical
storage, i.e. the conj/neg transform was applied twice (`conj(conj(x)) == x`).

`xpu -> xpu` being correct is consistent and expected: for a same-device copy
`copy_requires_temporaries` returns `false`, so the staging branch is never
entered. This matches the direction pattern upstream reported for ROCm
(96/128 failures for each CPU<->GPU direction, 0/128 for GPU->GPU).

## Root cause

`src/ATen/native/xpu/Copy.cpp`, inside the staging branch of `_copy_xpu`
(registered as `REGISTER_XPU_DISPATCH(copy_stub, &native::xpu::_copy_xpu)`):

```cpp
// line 221 (device-side / non_blocking branch)
src_contig = iter.tensor(1).to(iter.dtype(0)).expand_as(dst).contiguous();
// line 228 (host-side conversion branch)
src_contig = iter.tensor(1).expand_as(dst).contiguous();

// propagate the correct conjugate bit
dst_contig._set_conj(dst.is_conj());
src_contig._set_conj(iter.tensor(1).is_conj());   // line 233

dst_contig._set_neg(dst.is_neg());
src_contig._set_neg(iter.tensor(1).is_neg());     // line 236

// ...
dst_contig.copy_(src_contig, non_blocking);       // line 241
```

`.expand_as(dst)` makes the source non-contiguous (stride 0), so `.contiguous()`
materializes a real buffer. Materialization resolves the conj/neg view bits: the
temporary already holds the *logical* values and reports `is_conj() == false`.
Line 233/236 then re-assert the original bits on that temporary, which tells the
recursive `copy_` at line 241 that the already-resolved values still need the
transform. It is applied a second time, yielding the physical value.

The source temporary's own flags are already correct after `.contiguous()`; only
the destination's flags need propagating. Upstream's suggested fix (dropping the
two `src_contig._set_*` calls while keeping the `dst_contig` ones) applies
verbatim to this file, but it should be validated against the non-staging and
cross-XPU-device paths and against the `dst_contig.is_same(dst)` copy-back at
line 246 before landing.

## Target-path evidence

- The XPU destination/source tensors are on `xpu:0`; the log records
  `TARGET_PATH cpu_to_xpu dst_device=xpu:0 src_conj=True src_neg=False` and
  `TARGET_PATH xpu_to_cpu src_device=xpu:0 ...` for each case.
- The `xpu -> xpu` control in the same run is correct, which rules out a
  defect in the conj/neg view semantics themselves or in the XPU copy kernel,
  and isolates the failure to the staging branch.
- The failing value is bit-exactly the physical storage rather than an
  arbitrary wrong number, matching the double-application signature.
- The inputs are exactly representable, with no randomness, no reduction and no
  dtype conversion, so this is not a tolerance artifact.

## Reproducer

```python
import torch

z_cpu = torch.tensor([1 + 2j], dtype=torch.complex64)
for name, src in [("conjugate", z_cpu.conj()), ("negative", z_cpu.conj().imag)]:
    dst = torch.zeros(2, dtype=src.dtype, device="xpu")
    dst.copy_(src)  # broadcasts 1 -> 2, so a temporary is required
    torch.xpu.synchronize()
    print("cpu->xpu", name, "actual:", dst.cpu().tolist(),
          "expected:", src.resolve_conj().resolve_neg().expand(2).tolist())

z_xpu = torch.tensor([1 + 2j], dtype=torch.complex64, device="xpu")
for name, src in [("conjugate", z_xpu.conj()), ("negative", z_xpu.conj().imag)]:
    dst = torch.zeros(2, dtype=src.dtype)
    dst.copy_(src)
    torch.xpu.synchronize()
    print("xpu->cpu", name, "actual:", dst.tolist(),
          "expected:", src.resolve_conj().resolve_neg().expand(2).cpu().tolist())

# control: same-device copy takes no temporary and is correct
for name, src in [("conjugate", z_xpu.conj()), ("negative", z_xpu.conj().imag)]:
    dst = torch.zeros(2, dtype=src.dtype, device="xpu")
    dst.copy_(src)
    torch.xpu.synchronize()
    print("xpu->xpu", name, "actual:", dst.cpu().tolist())
```

## Output

```text
cpu->xpu conjugate: actual=[(1+2j), (1+2j)] expected=[(1-2j), (1-2j)] physical=[(1+2j), (1+2j)]
cpu->xpu negative: actual=[2.0, 2.0] expected=[-2.0, -2.0] physical=[2.0, 2.0]
xpu->cpu conjugate: actual=[(1+2j), (1+2j)] expected=[(1-2j), (1-2j)] physical=[(1+2j), (1+2j)]
xpu->cpu negative: actual=[2.0, 2.0] expected=[-2.0, -2.0] physical=[2.0, 2.0]
xpu->xpu conjugate: actual=[(1-2j), (1-2j)] expected=[(1-2j), (1-2j)] physical=[(1+2j), (1+2j)]
xpu->xpu negative: actual=[-2.0, -2.0] expected=[-2.0, -2.0] physical=[2.0, 2.0]
```

## Environment

| | |
|---|---|
| torch | `2.16.0.dev20261012+xpu` |
| python | 3.13.13 (`/opt/conda/bin/python3.13`) |
| torch path | `/opt/conda/lib/python3.13/site-packages/torch/__init__.py` |
| device | `Intel(R) Arc(TM) Pro B60 Graphics` (`xpu_available=true`) |

## Ownership rationale

The defective code is `src/ATen/native/xpu/Copy.cpp` in this repository, not
upstream PyTorch. Upstream issue #200613 is scoped to
`aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/Copy.cu`; a search of `pytorch/pytorch` found no
issue or PR that owns the XPU side, and a search of `intel/torch-xpu-ops`
(`conj`, `conjugate`, `resolve_conj`, `copy_ broadcast`, `Copy.cpp`,
`xpu-alignment` titles) found no existing tracker for this behavior.
Independent XPU work is therefore required and does not depend on any upstream
change landing.

*Filed by the xpu-alignment automation; evidence produced by a deterministic
runner and independently reviewed.*

The inputs are exactly representable, with no randomness, no reduction and no
dtype conversion, so this is not a tolerance artifact.

Reproducer
import torch

z_cpu = torch.tensor([1 + 2j], dtype=torch.complex64)
for name, src in [("conjugate", z_cpu.conj()), ("negative", z_cpu.conj().imag)]:
    dst = torch.zeros(2, dtype=src.dtype, device="xpu")
    dst.copy_(src)  # broadcasts 1 -> 2, so a temporary is required
    torch.xpu.synchronize()
    print("cpu->xpu", name, "actual:", dst.cpu().tolist(),
          "expected:", src.resolve_conj().resolve_neg().expand(2).tolist())

z_xpu = torch.tensor([1 + 2j], dtype=torch.complex64, device="xpu")
for name, src in [("conjugate", z_xpu.conj()), ("negative", z_xpu.conj().imag)]:
    dst = torch.zeros(2, dtype=src.dtype)
    dst.copy_(src)
    torch.xpu.synchronize()
    print("xpu->cpu", name, "actual:", dst.tolist(),
          "expected:", src.resolve_conj().resolve_neg().expand(2).cpu().tolist())

# control: same-device copy takes no temporary and is correct
for name, src in [("conjugate", z_xpu.conj()), ("negative", z_xpu.conj().imag)]:
    dst = torch.zeros(2, dtype=src.dtype, device="xpu")
    dst.copy_(src)
    torch.xpu.synchronize()
    print("xpu->xpu", name, "actual:", dst.cpu().tolist())

upstream PyTorch. Upstream issue #200613 is scoped to

issues.title: F.interpolate(mode="nearest") returns wrong values for channels_last input with more than 256 channels
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

On XPU, nearest upsampling gives wrong results when the input is channels_last and has more than 256 channels. Contiguous (NCHW) input is fine. It happens with fp16, bf16 and fp32. When it fails, almost every output element is wrong, in every channel. These are not small rounding differences.
```
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def matches_cpu(c, dtype=torch.float16):
    x = torch.randn(1, c, 8, 8).to(dtype).contiguous(memory_format=torch.channels_last)
    out = F.interpolate(x.xpu(), scale_factor=2.0, mode="nearest").cpu()
    ref = F.interpolate(x.float(), scale_factor=2.0, mode="nearest").to(dtype)
    return torch.equal(out, ref)

for c in (64, 128, 255, 256, 257, 384, 511, 512):
    print(c, matches_cpu(c))
print("fp32, C=512:", matches_cpu(512, torch.float32))
print("bf16, C=512:", matches_cpu(512, torch.bfloat16))
```
It seems to be a regression, as PT 2.14 is OK with this case

nodes.body: The channels-last nearest2d kernel capped the launch at 65,536 work-items, but each work-item handled only one element. With 16x16 output, C=257 exceeds that limit, leaving elements unwritten. A grid-stride loop fixes the coverage; the issue’s fp16, fp32, and bf16 comparisons now pass on my XPU setup. PR: [地址已移除：intel/torch-xpu-ops#5719]

### 🐛 Describe the bug with skip template

<!-- cases:begin -->
Cases:
xpu_profiling,third_party.torch-xpu-ops.test.profiling.test_llama_profiling.TestLlamaProfiling,test_gemm_kernel_calls_per_iteration

<!-- cases:end -->

### Summary

test_gemm_kernel_calls_per_iteration profiles llama.py and asserts the number of 'gemm_kernel' events per iteration against the pinned EXPECTED_GEMM_CALLS=226. The run counts 225, stably across all five profiled iterations ({0: 225, 1: 225, 2: 225, 3: 225, 4: 225}), so one GEMM launch has disappeared from the model's per-iteration kernel mix rather than the count being flaky; either the dispatch changed or the pinned expectation is stale.

nodes.body:
This error is caused by Transformers change in version v5.19.0, which changed Llama's RoPE matrix multiplication to elementwise multiplication here: [地址已移除：huggingface/transformers#49265]
Version of Transformers installed in CI is not controlled, without version pin.
CI logs confirm that v5.19.0 is the version of Transformers installed in CI.
In turn this caused number of gemm calls to drop by 1, exactly as reported in the ticket.


We have 2 solution paths for this:
- pin Transformers version to <5.19
- adjust expected value to match current Transformers implementation

Either way we should consider pinning dependencies' versions for CI runs, to avoid CI instabilities caused by such changes.

@daisyden Please help to find someone to make the decision on which way should we continue on this issue.

issues.title: [Bug Skip]: Profiler trace shows 56 overlapping GPU kernel pairs on a single XPU device timeline
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug with skip template

<!-- cases:begin -->
Cases:
xpu_profiling,third_party.torch-xpu-ops.test.profiling.test_for_overlapping_kernels.TestOverlappingKernels,test_overlapping_kernels

<!-- cases:end -->

### Summary

test_overlapping_kernels reads the rn50 chrome trace and requires that no two GPU-side events (kernel, gpu_memset; memcpy excluded) overlap in time by more than 1 us, since they execute serially on one device. The run finds 56 overlapping pairs, which points at the kernel timestamps the XPU profiler writes into the trace rather than at the workload.

### ErrorLog

#### AssertionError: Scalars are not equal!

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/__w/torch-xpu-ops/torch-xpu-ops/pytorch/third_party/torch-xpu-ops/test/profiling/test_for_overlapping_kernels.py", line 130, in test_overlapping_kernels
    self.assertEqual(
  File "/__w/torch-xpu-ops/torch-xpu-ops/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/torch/testing/_internal/common_utils.py", line 5101, in assertEqual
    raise error_metas.pop()[0].to_error(  # type: ignore[index]
AssertionError: Scalars are not equal!

Expected 0 but got 56.
Absolute difference: 56
Relative difference: inf
Found 56 overlapping kernel pairs!

To execute this test, run the following from the base repo dir:
    python test/profiling/test_for_overlapping_kernels.py TestOverlappingKernels.test_overlapping_kernels

This message can be suppressed by setting PYTORCH_PRINT_REPRO_ON_FAILURE=0
```

nodes.bodyText: @aostrowski-hbn Can you please prioritize? This is external dependeny on PTI

nodes.body:
**Root cause.** Not oneDNN, not the driver, and the kernels do not really overlap: the raw L0 device ticks never do. PTI converts device timestamps from CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW to CLOCK_REALTIME with an offset it re-samples each time it pushes a batch of records. While NTP slews the wall clock, batches pushed ~200 ms apart get offsets ~13 us apart (6-8 us on the CI runners), so back-to-back kernels on one in-order queue look overlapped. Reproduced with PTI 0.17, 1.1 and 1.2, and with a standalone SYCL+PTI reproducer. Duplicate: #5341.

**Plan.**
1. PTI fix: reported as PTI-550, related to the existing PTI-361.
2. Workaround in PyTorch's Kineto XPU plugin: [地址已移除：pytorch/pytorch#201856] It keeps PTI on MONOTONIC_RAW and maps times to the wall clock once per session. Locally the failing repro goes from 56 overlaps in every run to none.
3. Once that lands, close this issue and #5341, which un-mutes the case. A separate ~1-2 us PTI effect can still invert very small gaps. If `test_for_overlapping_kernels` fails again because of it, we track it in a new issue against PTI rather than reopening this one.

cc: @aostrowski-hbn @PawelSwider2000 (#5341, PTI-361)
